title: The first sustained orbit.
summary: Ship 41 reached Earth orbit and deployed 26 operational Starlink V3 satellites. An early deorbit brought it back north of Hawaii.

details.heading: Committing to orbit
details.body: Flight 14 began on a suborbital ascent profile so the ship could return even without an insertion burn. A vacuum Raptor shut down early, but controllers reviewed the vehicle’s condition and cleared it to continue. A short single-engine burn about 25 minutes after launch placed Ship 41 into sustained Earth orbit.

details.heading: The first orbital delivery
details.body: The dispenser released 26 operational Starlink V3 satellites between roughly 34 and 65 minutes after liftoff. Three carried additional cameras to examine the ship’s thermal protection. The shield also tested revised tile geometry and two tiles previously flown on Ship 40.

details.heading: A shorter flight, a different landing zone
details.body: The original plan called for six orbits and a Pacific return west of Chile. Controllers instead ordered an early deorbit around two hours and 12 minutes into flight. Starship completed a controlled splashdown north of Hawaii after about three hours and eight minutes, then tipped over and burned. Booster 21 had already completed its Gulf of Mexico return.

photo.alt: Starship Flight 14 campaign, photographed by Max Evans

timeline.event: Ship splashes down north of Hawaii

landings.note: Position published by @mcrs987 on 28 September 2026, 40 km downrange. He inferred an on-target landing from aircraft and vessel activity. This is an independent geolocation, rather than a position released from SpaceX telemetry.

Touchdown position published by @mcrs987 on 28 September 2026, about 500 km from the Hawaiian islands. He identified MELISSA C as the supporting vessel. The published digits are retained; positional accuracy was not stated.

analysis.title: Comparing the last three landing engines
analysis.summary: He mirrored the engine graphic and rotated camera views to compare plume directions consistently. He highlighted an unusually early and visually faint shutdown of one of the booster’s last three landing engines, while reporting that the other two completed their burns.

analysis.title: Ice forming around the booster raceway
analysis.summary: He highlighted apparent ice formation around the booster’s external raceway during the landing burn and compared it with footage from Flights 12 and 13. He questioned what could explain it without establishing a cause; a broken component is not treated as a confirmed finding.

analysis.title: Venting when the vacuum engine shut down
analysis.summary: He noticed aft-cavity venting around the ship’s vacuum-engine shutdown. The post considered nitrogen purge and propellant as possibilities, rather than identifying the vented material conclusively. Both possibilities remain unconfirmed in this analysis.

debrief.changed: Starship entered sustained orbit and delivered operational satellites.
debrief.worked: Twenty-six satellites deployed; both stages completed ocean returns.
debrief.fell_short: An ascent engine shut down early, and the planned six-orbit flight was shortened.

title: A ship that stayed afloat.
summary: Twenty working Starlink V3 satellites were tested on a suborbital path. Ship 40 landed softly and remained intact on the Indian Ocean.

details.heading: Working satellites, deliberately suborbital
details.body: Ship 40 released 20 working Starlink V3 satellites after completing ascent. SpaceX communicated with each using radio and laser links and downloaded telemetry. These were functional hardware tests, but the objects followed a deliberately suborbital path and reentered about 20 minutes after deployment.

details.heading: A complete upper-stage return
details.body: The ship restarted a Raptor in space, survived entry and performed a banking maneuver before a soft Indian Ocean splashdown. All three landing engines initially restarted. Booster 20 completed the high-thrust part of boostback but ended it early and suffered a hard splashdown after an incomplete landing-engine restart.

details.heading: An intact ship to examine
details.body: Ship 40 remained intact and afloat after tipping over, allowing close inspection of the heat shield. Recovery vessels tracked the drifting ship. It was subsequently taken to waters near Christmas Island, where engineers collected samples and data before it was loaded onto the heavy-lift vessel Forte in August.

photo.alt: Starship Flight 13 campaign, photographed by Max Evans

timeline.event: Booster impacts after incomplete landing burn

landings.note: Approximate splashdown position published by @mcrs987 on 25 July 2026, about 20 km from the intended target. He cited a smoke plume in GOES-19 imagery. This is the booster’s estimated position, not Ship 40’s landing or subsequent drift.

analysis.title: Locating Booster 20’s splashdown
analysis.summary: He estimated the booster’s splashdown at 25°56′43″N, 96°54′12″W, roughly 20 km from the intended location, and pointed to a smoke plume in GOES-19 imagery. The coordinate panel records this as a published estimate.

analysis.title: Following Ship 40’s drift and recovery fleet
analysis.summary: His tracking updates followed the floating ship and GO Australis, then the arrival of Normand Ranger. On 31 July, he reported about 403 km of drift over 162 hours. These are post-touchdown movements, not the ship’s initial landing coordinates.

debrief.changed: Working Starlink V3 satellites were tested on a suborbital path.
debrief.worked: Ship 40 relit a Raptor, landed softly and remained intact afloat.
debrief.fell_short: Booster 20 ended boostback early and suffered a hard splashdown.

title: V3 takes flight.
summary: New vehicles, Raptor 3 engines and Pad 2 debuted together. Ship 39 completed its return; Booster 19 impacted far beyond its landing target.

details.heading: A new propulsion generation
details.body: The first V3 mission also introduced Raptor 3 engines and Starbase’s second orbital launch pad. Ship 39 reached its planned suborbital trajectory despite a vacuum-engine shutdown during ascent. It deployed 20 Starlink V3 mass simulators and two modified Starlink satellites equipped for imaging.

details.heading: Deployment and a two-engine landing
details.body: The planned in-space relight was skipped. During return, the ship tested its aft-flap structure and a banking maneuver relevant to future returns to Starbase. It retained control through atmospheric entry, then flipped upright and completed an Indian Ocean splashdown using two Raptor engines.

details.heading: A booster return cut short
details.body: Booster 19 suffered engine-start failures during boostback and did not return to its intended near-coastal zone. Its hard impact occurred far downrange. A published geolocation estimate places it about 318 kilometers from launch and 310 kilometers from the intended landing target; the coordinates below identify that impact, rather than a successful landing.

photo.alt: Starship Flight 12 campaign, photographed by Max Evans

timeline.event: First V3 stack launches from Pad 2

landings.note: Approximate position published by @mcrs987 on 23 May 2026. About 318 km downrange and 310 km from the intended landing target. This marks the booster’s impact location; it is not the target or the ship’s splashdown.

analysis.title: Color-coding the boostback engine sequence
analysis.summary: He color-coded Booster 19’s engine startup and shutdown sequence to illustrate how one engine event affected the rest of the boostback. His post notes three other engines failing to fully ignite before the energetic event.

analysis.title: Finding the far-downrange booster impact
analysis.summary: He published an approximate Booster 19 impact position at 25°01′N, 94°10′W, about 318 km downrange and 310 km from the intended target. The recovery-geography panel preserves the published minute precision and links to a map. This is the impact estimate, not a successful landing.

debrief.changed: V3 vehicles, Raptor 3 engines and Pad 2 debuted together.
debrief.worked: Ship 39 deployed test payloads and completed a two-engine splashdown.
debrief.fell_short: The in-space relight was skipped; Booster 19 impacted far beyond its target.

title: Closing the V2 chapter.
summary: The final second-generation ship deployed eight simulators, restarted a Raptor and tested a banking maneuver before splashdown.

details.heading: A final V2 demonstration
details.body: Ship 38 completed the final second-generation Starship mission. It released eight Starlink mass simulators during coast and restarted a Raptor in space. As on Flight 10, the payloads were deliberately suborbital and did not remain in Earth orbit.

details.heading: Preparing a future return to Starbase
details.body: The ship tested its thermal protection during reentry and executed a dynamic banking maneuver to explore how future ships could return toward Starbase. It then completed its landing flip and controlled Indian Ocean splashdown, about 66 minutes after launch.

details.heading: Reuse on the first stage
details.body: Booster 15 flew for a second time after its Flight 8 catch. Its ocean return tested a landing-burn profile intended for the next generation of hardware. Both stages completed their main flight objectives, closing the V2 campaign ahead of the V3 vehicle and Raptor 3 debut.

photo.alt: Starship Flight 11 campaign, photographed by Max Evans

analysis.title: Ship 38’s descent over a virtual Starbase
analysis.summary: He reconstructed the Flight 11 descent and overlaid it on Starbase’s second launch tower to visualize a possible future return-to-launch-site catch. The real flight ended at sea; the tower overlay is a visualization, not an actual approach or catch attempt. A real-time 4K breakdown explains the reconstruction.

debrief.changed: The final V2 flight tested a banking maneuver for future returns.
debrief.worked: Eight simulators deployed, a Raptor relit, and both stages completed their objectives.
debrief.fell_short: Payloads remained deliberately suborbital; the ship was not recovered.

title: Payloads away.
summary: Eight simulators left the dispenser for the first time. An in-space relight and two controlled ocean returns completed the V2 mission profile.

details.heading: Completing the mission profile
details.body: Ship 37 completed ascent and released eight Starlink mass simulators, the first successful Starship payload deployment. The objects followed a suborbital trajectory and were intended to reenter. A Raptor was restarted during coast, demonstrating the relight capability again.

details.heading: A deliberately demanding return
details.body: The heat shield included deliberately missing tiles and experimental configurations. Starship endured substantial damage during entry but retained enough control for a landing flip and controlled Indian Ocean splashdown. This completed the upper-stage objectives that Flights 7, 8 and 9 had not reached.

details.heading: A backup-engine experiment
details.body: Booster 16 tested a backup landing-engine sequence before its planned ocean splashdown. Ship 37 had replaced Ship 36, which was destroyed during ground testing in June. Flight 10 returned the campaign to a complete ascent, coast and reentry demonstration.

photo.alt: Starship Flight 10 campaign, photographed by Max Evans

analysis.title: The ship attitude display as a timelapse
analysis.summary: He condensed the broadcast’s ship-attitude graphic into a short timelapse. It offers a continuous view of how the displayed orientation changed across the flight, using the webcast graphic rather than an independently measured trajectory.

analysis.title: Highlighting the departing heat-shield tiles
analysis.summary: He annotated imagery of Ship 37’s final descent to highlight objects trailing the vehicle, identifying them as heat-shield tiles. The image makes his observation easy to inspect, but it does not establish a complete tile-loss count or a detailed cause for each loss.

debrief.changed: Starship successfully deployed payload simulators for the first time.
debrief.worked: Eight simulators deployed, a Raptor relit, and both stages splashed down softly.
debrief.fell_short: The ship sustained substantial entry damage despite completing its return.

title: Super Heavy flies again.
summary: Booster 14 made the first Super Heavy reflight. Ship 35 completed ascent, then lost control during its coast toward the Indian Ocean.

details.heading: A flight-proven booster
details.body: Booster 14 returned to flight after its Flight 7 tower catch, marking the first reuse of a Super Heavy. This mission deliberately targeted an ocean return and a more demanding descent, rather than another catch. The booster was lost during its landing-burn test.

details.heading: The dispenser stays closed
details.body: Ship 35 completed its ascent burn and reached its intended suborbital trajectory. The payload door failed to open, preventing deployment of eight Starlink mass simulators. The flight nevertheless extended second-generation ship operation beyond the ascent failures of Flights 7 and 8.

details.heading: Coast without control
details.body: A propellant leak and subsequent attitude-control problem prevented the planned Raptor relight and controlled entry attitude. The ship was passivated and communications ended during its Indian Ocean return around 47 minutes after liftoff. A full V2 mission still remained to be completed.

photo.alt: Starship Flight 9 campaign, photographed by Max Evans

analysis.title: Locating the start of the booster anomaly
analysis.summary: Using SpaceX and ground footage, he placed the initial Booster 14-2 explosion in the aft section and considered a hard engine shutdown as a possible trigger. That is a proposed mechanism from visible evidence, not a confirmed diagnosis. His initial speed estimate was subsequently corrected, so it is not repeated here.

analysis.title: Predicting the intended ocean-return zone
analysis.summary: Before launch, he tracked Hannah Ray toward the roughly 30 km offshore area associated with Booster 13, rather than the farther-out Booster 11 zone. This was a prediction of the intended landing area from vessel movement; it is not the location where Booster 14-2 was actually lost.

debrief.changed: Booster 14 made the first Super Heavy reflight.
debrief.worked: Ship 35 completed ascent, extending V2 operation beyond Flights 7 and 8.
debrief.fell_short: The payload door stayed closed; both stages were lost on return.

title: A catch amid a setback.
summary: Booster 15 became the third Super Heavy caught at Starbase. Ship 34 lost engines and attitude control before completing ascent.

details.heading: A second V2 upper stage
details.body: Flight 8 repeated the second-generation ship’s attempt to complete ascent and test its payload dispenser. Before launch, a 60-second static fire explored engine operating conditions and hardware changes following Flight 7. Four Starlink mass simulators remained aboard when the flight ended.

details.heading: The booster reaches the tower
details.body: Booster 15 completed its return and was caught by the tower around seven minutes after launch. This was the third successful Super Heavy catch, even though some engines failed to restart during the return sequence.

details.heading: A different engine failure
details.body: Ship 34 suffered an aft-section event followed by multiple engine shutdowns and loss of attitude control. Telemetry ended before the planned in-space operations. SpaceX attributed the initiating event to a hardware failure in a center Raptor engine; payload deployment and controlled reentry were not demonstrated.

photo.alt: Starship Flight 8 campaign, photographed by Max Evans

timeline.event: Ship loses engines and attitude control

analysis.title: Rebuilding Ship 34’s final flight
analysis.summary: He produced a 3D reconstruction of Flight 8’s breakup using multiple available views. The animation combines engine-state information and camera perspectives to make the loss of orientation and subsequent breakup easier to follow.

analysis.title: Stabilizing the breakup footage
analysis.summary: He manually stabilized his footage and identified the visible detonation at approximately T+9 minutes 30 seconds. This is his video timing estimate; the mission timeline remains approximate rather than implying frame-perfect agreement across different recordings.

debrief.changed: The V2 campaign repeated its ascent and dispenser test attempt.
debrief.worked: Booster 15 returned for the third Super Heavy catch.
debrief.fell_short: Ship engine failures and loss of attitude control ended ascent.

title: The second-generation debut.
summary: A redesigned ship entered flight testing. Booster 14 returned to the tower, but an aft-section fire ended Ship 33’s ascent.

details.heading: More capacity, new hardware
details.body: Ship 33 introduced the second-generation upper stage, with larger propellant tanks, revised avionics and smaller forward flaps moved away from the hottest part of the flow. Ten Starlink mass simulators were carried for a deployment test, but never released.

details.heading: A booster recovered again
details.body: Super Heavy completed its boostback and returned to the tower for the program’s second catch. Booster 14 survived the flight and later became the first Super Heavy to launch again, on Flight 9.

details.heading: The upper-stage investigation
details.body: The ship lost engines and communications during ascent, about eight and a half minutes after launch. SpaceX’s investigation linked the failure to stronger-than-expected vibration, propellant leaks and an aft-section fire. Debris descended over the Caribbean, and the planned coast, deployment and reentry experiments were not reached.

analysis.title: A preliminary 3D breakup sequence
analysis.summary: He reconstructed Ship 33’s motion from the first engine problems to breakup, using onboard views and later ground footage. His methodology explicitly notes a lack of data after loss of signal and before breakup, so the intervening orientation is estimated.

analysis.title: A longer failure-timeline study
analysis.summary: A later 26-post thread assembled a proposed engine-failure, fire, loss-of-signal and debris timeline. It includes a geolocation exercise using several breakup videos, but expressly allows that its explanation may be wrong. Its detailed failure mechanisms are hypotheses, separate from SpaceX’s investigation.

debrief.changed: The second-generation ship introduced larger tanks and revised flaps.
debrief.worked: Booster 14 returned for the program’s second tower catch.
debrief.fell_short: An aft-section fire ended ship ascent before deployment and reentry tests.

title: A restart above Earth.
summary: Starship restarted a Raptor in space for the first time and returned in daylight. Super Heavy diverted safely from the tower.

details.heading: An offshore diversion
details.body: Flight 6 was the last mission for the first-generation Starship upper stage. Booster 13 was initially intended to return to the tower, but the catch was called off after a tower-system problem. The booster instead performed a controlled Gulf of Mexico splashdown.

details.heading: The engine relight milestone
details.body: Ship 31 restarted a single Raptor during coast, demonstrating an engine operation needed for future orbital insertion and deorbit burns. This was a relight demonstration on a suborbital flight, rather than a commitment to a sustained Earth orbit.

details.heading: Testing the edge of the envelope
details.body: The ship tested altered heat-shield coverage and a more demanding entry profile. It completed a landing flip and soft Indian Ocean splashdown in daylight, giving clearer views of the final descent. A plush banana stayed aboard as the mission’s zero-gravity indicator.

photo.alt: Starship Flight 6 campaign, photographed by Max Evans

analysis.title: Counting the tiles removed from Ship 31
analysis.summary: After comparing heat-shield imagery, he counted 1,370 removed tiles and calculated a reduction from 18,492 to 17,122. These are his image-based counts, not a SpaceX inventory. His earlier comparison visualizes the altered coverage ahead of Flight 6.

analysis.title: Tracking the booster after splashdown
analysis.summary: The day after Flight 6, he reported that Booster 13 had been sunk and that both nearby vessels had left the area. This is a post-landing status report and does not establish a precise touchdown position.

debrief.changed: The ship demonstrated its first Raptor relight in space.
debrief.worked: Both stages completed controlled splashdowns, with the ship returning in daylight.
debrief.fell_short: A tower-system problem called off the planned booster catch.

title: Caught on the first attempt.
summary: The launch tower caught Booster 12. Ship 30 completed its own return to a precisely targeted Indian Ocean splashdown.

details.heading: Returning to the launch tower
details.body: For the first booster catch, Super Heavy returned to Starbase rather than an offshore splashdown zone. Vehicle and tower health checks had to pass before the return was authorized. Booster 12 slowed beside the tower and settled onto its mechanical arms about seven minutes after launch.

details.heading: An upgraded thermal shield
details.body: Ship 30 flew with revised heat-shield tiles and a backup ablative layer. It completed its suborbital coast and atmospheric return, then relit its landing engines for a controlled splashdown in the Indian Ocean. A pre-positioned camera buoy filmed the final descent at night.

details.heading: Two very different recoveries
details.body: The booster was recovered at the launch site, while the ship was intentionally expended at sea and burned after tipping over. The tower catch demonstrated a central part of the planned reuse system; recovering an upper stage remained a separate challenge.

photo.alt: Starship Flight 5 campaign, photographed by Max Evans

timeline.event: Ship splashes down beside camera buoy

landings.note: Estimated ring location published by @mcrs987 on 15 October 2024, using video and offshore vessel activity. He quoted a ±0.5 km margin. This marks the discarded adapter, rather than a booster or ship landing.

analysis.title: A trajectory drawn from video frames
analysis.summary: He combined frames from one of his Flight 5 videos into a simulated long exposure. The result makes the vehicle’s path easier to see in one image; it is a frame composite, not a photograph made with a single long exposure.

analysis.title: Examining an experimental coated tile
analysis.summary: While aligning the livestream into a continuous timelapse, he highlighted a bright aluminum-coated tile on Ship 30 and interpreted its appearance as melting. The post supplies a useful close look at a heat-shield experiment; the thermal interpretation is his observation from the footage.

debrief.changed: The booster returned to the tower for its first catch.
debrief.worked: Booster 12 was caught; Ship 30 reached its targeted splashdown zone.
debrief.fell_short: The ship was intentionally expended at sea; upper-stage recovery remained ahead.

title: Two stages. Two splashdowns.
summary: Super Heavy and Starship both completed controlled ocean descents for the first time, despite severe damage to a ship flap.

details.heading: Bringing the booster back
details.body: Booster 11 completed ascent, boostback and a landing burn before a soft splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico. The hot-stage ring was jettisoned after separation to reduce the mass carried through the return. The booster’s ocean landing provided a rehearsal for a future tower catch.

details.heading: A damaged flap keeps working
details.body: Ship 29 survived atmospheric entry even as heating visibly eroded a forward flap and damaged its camera view. The remaining structure and control authority were sufficient to guide the ship through descent, ignite the landing engines and execute the flip to a vertical attitude.

details.heading: The foundation for a catch
details.body: The ship splashed down in the Indian Ocean roughly 66 minutes after launch. Neither stage was intended to be recovered intact, but both completed their controlled return sequences. Surviving reentry was the key advance over Flight 3.

analysis.title: Visualizing the damaged forward flap
analysis.summary: He created a short CG recreation of Ship 29’s landing flip to show his interpretation of the damaged forward flap’s movement. His description proposed complete detachment of the Y+ forward flap; the reconstruction should be read as an interpretation of footage, rather than an official structural assessment.

analysis.title: Following the Booster 11 recovery vessel
analysis.summary: In September, he tracked HOS Ridgewind lingering near his estimated Booster 11 splashdown area. He distinguished the vessel’s position from the estimated landing point and considered possible debris drift. A later post reported that booster debris was being recovered from the Gulf.

debrief.changed: Both stages demonstrated controlled ocean descents.
debrief.worked: The ship retained control through entry despite severe flap damage.
debrief.fell_short: A forward flap suffered significant thermal damage; neither vehicle was recovered intact.

title: Through the plasma.
summary: A full ascent burn, a payload-door test and an internal propellant transfer. Reentry ended the ship’s first extended spaceflight.

details.heading: A full-duration burn
details.body: Ship 28 completed its ascent burn and entered a long coast toward the Indian Ocean. Its trajectory deliberately intersected the atmosphere, allowing a return without first entering a stable orbit. Live onboard views showed the curvature of Earth and plasma forming during descent.

details.heading: Working during coast
details.body: During coast, Starship opened and closed its payload door and demonstrated a transfer of liquid oxygen between onboard tanks. This was an internal transfer experiment, an early step toward managing cryogenic propellant in space. A planned Raptor relight was skipped because of the ship’s roll.

details.heading: The return remained unfinished
details.body: Booster 10 failed to complete its landing burn. The ship also lost attitude control and broke up during reentry, with communications ending around 49 minutes after launch. Both ascent and in-space experiments progressed further than on the preceding flight.

photo.alt: Starship Flight 3 campaign, photographed by Max Evans

analysis.title: Reconstructing Booster 10’s orientation
analysis.summary: He aligned a booster descent model to onboard camera views and added a rough trajectory with atmospheric drag. The reconstruction was labeled a work in progress. He used it to explore whether the boostback thrust direction contributed to the booster’s underperformance.

analysis.title: A thrust-direction hypothesis, corrected
analysis.summary: His interpretation was that much of the boostback thrust pointed across the direction of travel, reducing its useful component. A follow-up corrected his wording from “parallel” to “perpendicular.” This remains his proposed explanation from a preliminary reconstruction, not an established mission finding.

debrief.changed: The ship completed its first full ascent burn and extended coast.
debrief.worked: Payload-door operation and internal liquid-oxygen transfer were demonstrated.
debrief.fell_short: The relight was skipped; neither stage completed its return.

title: Separation. Then space.
summary: The first hot-stage separation sent Ship 25 above the atmosphere. Both stages were lost before their planned returns.

details.heading: A different way to separate
details.body: All 33 booster engines operated through ascent. Starship then ignited its engines while still attached to Super Heavy, pushing the stages apart through a newly added vented hot-stage ring. This demonstrated the separation method that became standard on later flights.

details.heading: Two separate failures
details.body: Booster 9 was lost during its boostback sequence. Ship 25 continued to an altitude of about 149 kilometers, but did not complete its ascent burn. SpaceX linked its loss to a fire associated with venting excess liquid oxygen near the end of ascent.

details.heading: A longer view of ascent
details.body: The flight lasted about eight minutes for the ship, more than twice the first integrated test’s duration. It demonstrated hot staging and extended upper-stage operation, while leaving controlled reentry, payload operations and vehicle recovery for later missions.

photo.alt: Starship Flight 2 campaign, photographed by Max Evans

timeline.event: Ship lost near the end of ascent

analysis.title: Inside the tanks during hot staging
analysis.summary: A cutaway animation combines internal propellant motion, vehicle orientation and engine activity during separation and the booster’s flip. He explicitly described the render as imperfect: it illustrates possible propellant motion during the maneuver, rather than proving a failure cause or reproducing SpaceX’s internal simulation.

debrief.changed: Hot staging introduced a new separation method.
debrief.worked: All 33 booster engines operated through ascent; hot staging succeeded.
debrief.fell_short: Both stages were lost before completing their planned returns.

title: The first integrated flight.
summary: Booster 7 and Ship 24 flew together for the first time. The stack cleared the pad, but never separated.

details.heading: A complete stack, at last
details.body: This was the first launch of a complete Starship system: the methane-fueled Super Heavy booster beneath the Starship upper stage. Earlier prototypes had tested the ship’s atmospheric descent and landing separately. The integrated vehicle lifted off from Starbase and began climbing over the Gulf of Mexico.

details.heading: An ascent cut short
details.body: Several booster engines stopped during ascent. The stack lost control, tumbled and failed to separate, so Ship 24 never began its own powered flight. The flight termination system destroyed both stages roughly four minutes after launch; neither vehicle reached its planned ocean return.

details.heading: The next iteration
details.body: The launch also damaged the concrete beneath the mount. Subsequent flights introduced a water-cooled steel plate and deluge system, alongside changes to the vehicle and flight termination system. The mission established the starting point for testing the two stages together.

photo.alt: Starship Flight 1 campaign, photographed by Max Evans

analysis.title: The ground debris field
analysis.summary: In November 2024, he shared a Flight 1 debris-field map within a review of Fish and Wildlife Service records obtained through FOIA. The map distinguishes vehicle debris, concrete and Fondag material around the launch area. This is a retrospective document review, rather than an analysis posted during the flight.

debrief.changed: First flight of the integrated Ship and Super Heavy stack.
debrief.worked: The complete stack lifted off and cleared the launch pad.
debrief.fell_short: Engine losses and loss of control prevented stage separation.
